section_summary: This section documents international diplomatic reporting, foreign press reactions, and detailed official chronicles of the February 26, 1936 military insurrection in Tokyo (the February 26 Incident). It includes French newspaper analyses transmitted via Paris on the political and international significance of the assassinations, as well as an Istanbul Embassy memorandum of conversation with a Japanese diplomat reflecting the views of the army's young officer faction. The central document is a comprehensive day-by-day chronicle by United States Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo (Despatch No. 1721), reviewed by State Department Far Eastern Affairs officers, recounting the rebellion, martial law measures, Premier Keisuke Okada's escape, the surrender of insurgent troops, and contemporary Japanese press and official bulletins.

subfiles.about: French press clippings and translated commentaries published immediately following the February 26 Incident in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: A collection of press extracts from Parisian newspapers published on February 27, 1936, analyzing the military uprising and assassinations in Tokyo. The articles include commentaries from Le Petit Parisien, Le Populaire, L'Ère Nouvelle, L'Œuvre, Le Matin, Le Figaro, Le Jour, and L'Intransigeant. The commentators examine the conflict between civilian parliamentary leaders and ultranationalist military officers, the radical anti-capitalist and agrarian tenets of the young officer movement, and the potential repercussions for Japanese policy toward China, the Soviet Union, and the Western powers.
subfiles.title: Enclosures to Despatch Transmitting French Press Comment on the Tokyo Military Coup d'État of February 26, 1936

subfiles.about: State Department Far Eastern Affairs routing memorandum summarizing Istanbul Despatch No. 920.
subfiles.summary: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum commenting on Istanbul Embassy Despatch No. 920. The memorandum highlights a conversation between Second Secretary S. Walter Washington and Second Secretary Otosugu Saito of the Japanese Embassy at Istanbul following the Tokyo assassinations. It notes that Saito represents the Japanese foreign office faction aligned with the political reform program of the young army officers and shared their standard arguments.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Istanbul Despatch No. 920
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Maxwell M. Hamilton, Wallace T. Townsend

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch from Istanbul transmitting a memorandum of conversation with Japanese Embassy Secretary Otosugu Saito regarding the Tokyo uprising.
subfiles.from: G. Howland Shaw, Chargé d'Affaires a.i., American Embassy, Istanbul, Turkey
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 920 from Istanbul enclosing an extensive memorandum of conversation held on February 28, 1936, between Second Secretary S. Walter Washington and Japanese Second Secretary Otosugu Saito. Saito defended the young officers' revolt as an inevitable reaction against corrupt civilian politicians and argued that their goals were focused on domestic economic and social reorganization rather than foreign aggression. Saito maintained that the Emperor privately sympathized with the militarists, discussed relations with China, Russia, and the United States, and reacted with visible distress when a radio broadcast confirmed the death of Finance Minister Korekiyo Takahashi.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 920 from Istanbul Transmitting Memorandum of Conversation between S. Walter Washington and Otosugu Saito

subfiles.about: State Department Far Eastern Affairs memorandum evaluating Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1721.
subfiles.summary: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum assessing Despatch No. 1721 from the American Embassy in Tokyo. The memorandum praises the despatch as a detailed and well-prepared record of the Tokyo uprising up to March 6, noting that it recounts the military suppression measures starting on page 9. It also draws attention to a statement by a Japanese army captain that the wider army shared the rebels' sentiments while still adhering to discipline.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1721
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Maxwell M. Hamilton, Wallace T. Townsend

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic chronicle by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew detailing the events, suppression, aftermath, and documentation of the February 26 uprising in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo, Japan
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1721 from Tokyo providing an authoritative chronological narrative of the military revolt of February 26, 1936, through noon of March 6. It recounts the rebel raids on high officials, the assassinations of Viscount Saito, General Watanabe, and Colonel Matsuo (mistaken for Premier Okada), the mortal wounding of Takahashi and severe injury of Admiral Suzuki, the rebel manifestos, the establishment of martial law under Lieutenant General Kohei Kashii, and the eventual surrender of rebel troops under Imperial command. The despatch further details the survival and escape of Premier Okada, subsequent Cabinet and military resignations, new appointments, and efforts by Koki Hirota to form a government, accompanied by attached enclosures (1 through 9) comprising newspaper clippings, martial law proclamations, surrender leaflets, and Cabinet announcements.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1721: Chronicle of the Events of the February 26, 1936, Uprising Through Noon of March 6, 1936
